principles: Concord standards are commercial interoperability standards, not a universal government.
Local jurisdictions control criminal law, customs, landing permission, labor rules and resource claims.
Ship registry, port jurisdiction, contract venue and physical location can all matter to the same dispute.
Most captains encounter law through paperwork, inspection, fees and insurance rather than courtroom drama.

documents.name: Ship Registry Certificate
documents.purpose: Identifies legal vessel, registry jurisdiction and owner/operator.

documents.name: Cargo Manifest
documents.purpose: Declares commodity, quantity, ownership, hazard class and destination.

documents.name: Crew and Passenger Manifest
documents.purpose: Required for immigration, rescue planning and life-support compliance.

documents.name: Hazard Declaration
documents.purpose: Required before docking with chemical, biological, radiological, pressure or other regulated cargo.

documents.name: Survey Filing
documents.purpose: Records intended route, reserves and return window for supported frontier expeditions; mandatory only in some jurisdictions but strongly encouraged by insurers.

documents.name: Salvage Notice
documents.purpose: Records discovery/recovery circumstances before title is adjudicated.

jurisdictions.character: Dense regulation, excellent electronic processing, serious penalties for undeclared cargo.
Predictable documentation and arbitration; inspectors care intensely about standards compliance.
Business-friendly but strict about unsafe ships entering crowded yard traffic.
Focused on mass declarations, claim ownership and keeping improvised mining operations from endangering habitats.
Pragmatic outer-region enforcement. Paperwork is efficient because congestion is expensive.
Rules change quickly as a mining camp becomes a permanent jurisdiction. Claim and storage disputes dominate.
Light bureaucracy for ordinary freight, meticulous records for outbound expeditions and biological samples.
